props.title: Pulse
props.initialSlug: Technology unleashes a ghostly epidemic in Tokyo

sections.content: Pulse (2001) represents director Kiyoshi Kurosawa's masterful exploration of technological isolation and digital horror. Released just as internet adoption was exploding in Japan, it predicted our current social media alienation with haunting accuracy. The film's ghosts infiltrating the internet prefigured similar technological horror in The Ring (2002) and One Missed Call (2003), but Pulse digs deeper into existential dread rather than relying on jump scares. Its washed-out colors and empty urban spaces created a template for digital-age horror that influenced films like Unfriended (2014) and Host (2020).

sections.content: The film's influence on contemporary horror can't be overstated. Its vision of technology as a conduit for loneliness rather than connection influenced Searching (2018) and Profile (2018). The way it frames empty urban spaces and technological interfaces as sources of horror established visual language that Follow (2015) and Cam (2018) would later adopt. Even non-horror films like Her (2013) echo Pulse's concerns about technology's role in human isolation. SUBHEAD: The New Wave of Japanese Digital Horror

Pulse kicked off a wave of Japanese horror examining technology's dark side. Films like Suicide Club (2001) and Circuit (2001) followed similar themes but couldn't match its philosophical depth. The American remake Pulse missed the original's subtle commentary on urban alienation, focusing instead on standard ghost story tropes. Recent films like Don't Click (2020) and Countdown (2019) continue mining similar territory but rarely achieve Pulse's devastating portrait of modern loneliness.
